sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Wireless communication systems have accomplished total infiltration of personal life 
domains while establishing themselves as fundamental behavioural components for per -
sonal and professional operations. Wireless communications demand has dramatically 
increased throughout the past decades, creating a deficiency of radio spectrum below 10 
GHz according to Hass et al. [1]. This shortage, combined with the growing electromag -
netic interference (EMI) challenges in sensitive environments like hospitals, has driven 
the search for alternative, high-capacity, and interference-free communication methods.
Based on the past work on Optical Wireless Communication (OWC), this paper has 
covered in detail the Free-Space Optical (FSO) systems, for outdoor, high-speed, and 
weather-resistant use. Prior work involves simulation modeling of FSO systems to opti -
mize performance [ 2], hybrid FSO/RF networks to implement reliable inter-building 
links in poor conditions [ 3], and application of artificial intelligence to assess environ -
ment impacts, like haze [ 4] and snow [ 5], to link performance. Although FSO functions 
primarily in an outdoor setting and LiFi is an indoor application, both technologies 
share the same basic OWC principles- the use of the optical spectrum as a secure, high-
capacity, and interference-free means of communication. Building on this expertise, the 
present work applies FSO optimization strategies to LiFi system design for hospital envi-
ronments, addressing similar challenges such as channel impairments, BER reduction, 
and spectral efficiency enhancement under controlled indoor conditions. Visible light 
communication establishes itself as a new-generation wireless communication system 
that attracts expanding research interest. VLC takes advantage of universally available 
light, which is license-free, to provide an unparalleled spectrum resource and an efficient 
electromagnetic interference protection scheme that establishes a unique solution for 
wireless communication spectrum congestion. In LiFi, this is achieved through visible 
and infrared light-based downlink and uplink transmission, ensuring secure, high-speed, 
and bi-directional communication. A downlink and uplink communication procedure 
of LiFi operates through visible and infrared light emission and provides secure, high-
speed, bi-directional wireless communication [ 1, 6]. People using traditional radio wave 
transmission experience data speed limitations that visible light transmission can over -
come substantially by 100 times [7].
Recent research [6, 7] highlights the growing potential of VLC in medical applications. 
Unlike RF-based systems, VLC provides stable and efficient data transmission while pre-
venting electromagnetic interference with critical medical devices. This makes it partic -
ularly suitable for hospital environments where EMI-sensitive equipment, such as MRI 
scanners and pacemakers, is commonly used. Due to strict EMI and safety regulations, 
the current work focuses on hospital settings; however, the suggested LiFi architecture 
can also be used for broader IoT-based indoor networks, such as smart buildings, indus -
try automation, and healthcare IoT systems. The inability of light to penetrate walls 
enables visible light communication to automatically protect medical data by ensuring 
both security and privacy. These inherent properties position LiFi as a natural candidate 
for meeting the stringent requirements of hospital communication systems, including 
low latency, high data rate, and safety compliance [ 6, 7]. Latest developments in optical 
wireless systems serve as an additional incentive to LiFi-driven hospital communication 
systems. The works of Ali et al. [ 8] and Zayed et al. [ 9] show that there is substantial 
advancement in the modeling of LED-based optical links, spectral optimization, and 
Page 3 of 21
Sharma et al. Discover Computing           (2026) 29:30 
Lambertian-based channel analysis, which implicate the significance of wavelength 
selection and optical efficiency in high-performance communication links. These results 
confirm the relevance of the creation of safe, reliable, and efficient LiFi systems to highly 
sensitive indoor settings, including hospitals.
Current healthcare networks experience digital transformation through AI diagnos -
tic systems coupled with real-time telemedicine practices, along with high-resolution 
medical imaging solutions (that include 4 K surgical video streaming) [ 10]. Medical 
applications require wireless systems to preserve multi-gigabit data functionality along -
side ultra-low latency (10 milliseconds) performance and electromagnetic interference 
protection for safe integration with crucial medical devices, including MRI scanners, 
along with pacemakers and infusion pumps [ 1]. RF-based technologies, including WiFi 
and 5G, encounter performance obstacles when used within hospital buildings. WiFi in 
particular can cause EMI, lacks the necessary bandwidth for very large medical image 
transfers, and cannot guarantee uninterrupted low-latency performance in critical care 
scenarios. The medical telemetry systems that operate at 608–614 MHz could experi -
ence interference from WiFi systems, which use the 2.4/5 GHz bands. In addition, WiFi 
demonstrates insufficient bandwidth to manage Digital Imaging and Communications 
in Medicine (DICOM) image transfers larger than 1 GB per study [ 11]. Therefore, the 
healthcare industry requires urgent implementation of EMI-resistant wireless networks 
that meet its specific capacity requirements.
LiFi technology has proven itself as a revolutionary substitute for WiFi through its 
capacity to transmit data via visible light waves. The terahertz bandwidth of LiFi, as 
well as its built-in wall-penetrating security and complete electromagnetic interfer -
ence protection, makes it suitable for hospital use [ 12]. The EU’s ELIoT project dem -
onstrates micro-LED technology capabilities by reaching 10 Gbps data transfer speeds 
[13]. However, deploying LiFi in hospital environments requires addressing unique chal-
lenges such as maintaining signal integrity under patient and equipment movement, 
minimizing ambient light interference, and ensuring biological safety during prolonged 
operation. Signal integrity suffers from major deterioration during changing channel 
conditions, where patient movement combined with mobile medical tools and chang -
ing environmental light levels becomes an issue. LED wavelengths must be carefully 
selected to minimize tissue absorption since improper choice could cause localized heat-
ing, which affects biological safety during videoendoscopic procedures. Scientists recog -
nized that green light at 500 nm with an absorption coefficient (µabs) equal to 0.03 mm⁻¹ 
as a safer illumination, according to research [ 14]. They proved that green LEDs (500 
nm) possess a reduced tissue absorption coefficient compared to red or infrared alterna -
tives, thus demonstrating their safety advantages for healthcare applications based on 
LiFi technology. The IEC 62,471 standards are met while protecting user health during 
operations [14]. Typical medical devices must meet two critical standards: IEC 60601-
1-2 electromagnetic interference (EMI) requirements and HIPAA specifications for data 
security to safeguard patient records [ 15]. Our proposed system is designed to comply 
with these standards while delivering measurable improvements in BER, spectral effi -
ciency, and reliability.
High-speed data transmission represents a key feature of LiFi technology that is 
needed for communication in healthcare facilities, besides reducing electromag -
netic interference (EMI). Research conducted by Koonen [ 16] showed that indoor

sections.title: 2 Methodology and system design
sections.text:
This section describes the simulation-based methodology employed in designing, opti -
mizing, and comparing the proposed 4QAM-OFDM LiFi system to operate and per -
form well in electromagnetic interference (EMI) sensitive areas, such as a hospital. The 
approach is designed keeping in mind high reliability, biological safety, and better per -
formance than current systems, with reproducibility of a future study.
This study employs a simulation-driven approach to design and optimize a 4QAM-
OFDM-based LiFi system for EMI-sensitive hospital environments, as shown in Fig. 1. 
The methodology integrates OptiSystem™ 21 optical simulations and MATLAB R2024b-
based mathematical modelling to evaluate system performance through bit error rate 
(BER), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and latency [ 2, 4]. A LiFi system contains three fun -
damental components, comprising the transmitter module and optical wireless channel 
along with the receiver module.
A 4QAM-OFDM modulator with 1024 subcarriers and a 64-sample cyclic prefix (CP) 
function is used in the transmitter to mitigate inter-symbol interference (ISI). The sys -
tem utilizes a 500 nm LED optical source that satisfies IEC 62,471 photobiological safety

requirements by functioning with a modulation bandwidth of 100 MHz while the oper -
ating optical power is adjusted between 10 dBm and 30 dBm. Phosphor-converted LEDs 
can demonstrate electro-optical responses that reach down to sub-GHz band frequen -
cies under controlled laboratory conditions, although the practical modulation band -
width of the current work is 100 MHz. This is the value that represents the bandwidth 
constraints of the commercially available LED drivers, and it guarantees a single system 
design and an internal consistency in deploying the system to real hospitals. Operation 
at higher bandwidth (closely reaching hundreds of MHz to 1 GHz) will also be explored 
in the process of hardware prototyping. The optical source, which is modelled in this 
paper, is a phosphor-converted green LED that is appropriate to use in hospitals and that 
meets the IEC 62,471 photobiological safety standards. The 100 MHz band of modula -
tion corresponds to the high-speed phosphor LEDs in recent VLC literature. The maxi -
mum input of 30 dBm is only employed in simulation stress-testing to test performance 
in long distances and under the negative conditions of the channel. The real-life imple -
mentation would be at much lower optical power levels to adhere to the entirety of the 
IEC 62,471 and IEC 60,825 optical safety standards. The modification of the modula -
tion index ranges between 0.4 and 1.0, enabling maximum LED power efficiency as well 
as linear performance. The layout contains a DC bias driver circuit that helps minimize 
nonlinearity effects.
The model of the optical wireless channel demonstrates hospital environment charac -
teristics while exploring distances of 5 m to 25 m. The choice of longer link distances is 
because modern hospital wards, ICUs, operating theatres and corridor-based monitor -
ing rooms tend to be characterized by a ceiling-to-bed spacing that is longer than the 
average LiFi indoor range. Assessment of distances up to 25 m can be used to determine 
the limits of coverage and the worst-case attenuation characteristics. The propagation 
delay of such distances is still within the range of nanoseconds and can be ignored by 
the duration of the OFDM symbol, so the real-time medical communication will not be 
affected. The model uses a Lambertian radiation pattern to represent direct line-of-sight 
transmission. The paper is based on a perfect LOS setup. The actual situations in the 
hospital rooms, however, can be subjected to partial or complete NLOS states because 
of equipment, patient movement, and reflective surfaces. This has been recognised as a 
limitation, and future research will include ray-tracing and NLOS channel modelling to 
test more realistic hospital settings. The existing simulation model does not explicitly 
Fig. 1 4QAM-OFDM-based LiFi system block diagram
 
Page 7 of 21
Sharma et al. Discover Computing           (2026) 29:30 
simulate LED nonlinearities, shot noise, multipath bounces and the time variation due to 
human movement. The impairments are purposefully omitted to isolate an ideal optical 
system, whereby the behavior of baseline OFDM-QAM is observed. Subsequent work 
will include the addition of LED nonlinear models, contribution of shot-noise, RIN, mul-
tipath ray-tracing, and dynamic channel effects in order to be more representative of 
actual hospital LiFi deployments. The model represents ambient noise, which originates 
from fluorescent lighting, through a Gaussian distribution with − 50 dBm/Hz power 
density. The Beer-Lambert law (α = 0.2 dB/m) models the path loss, whereas an opti -
cal bandpass filter (centered at 500 nm) is employed at the receiver to diminish ambi -
ent light interference. This α = 0.2 dB/m corresponds to that of indoor VLC attenuation 
experimentally reported in optical wireless as short-range propagation, where the atten -
uation is largely affected by wall and medical surface absorption and scattering. Haas 
et al. have supported this range [ 26]. This is in line with the indoor VLC measurement 
studies, which have indicated attenuation coefficients of 0.15–0.25 dB/m in a normal 
hospital and office with moderate surface reflectivity. The current model then assumes 
the use of 0.2 dB/m as a central value. A more realistic characterization of path-loss, 
such as realistic multipath propagation and reflections off medical equipment, walls, 
and reflective surfaces, will be done in subsequent hardware experiments, through ray-
tracing and empirical calibration. Optimization of beam divergence angles within a 1 to 
4 mrad range accomplishes both high signal integrity and adequate coverage. The range 
of divergence angle of 1–4 mrad is informed by the common collimation properties that 
have been reported on phosphor LEDs in VLC studies. This is the assumed value of the 
simulation and will be experimentally confirmed with actual measured half-power beam 
angles and radiation patterns in a later hardware implementation.
The receiver module contains an optical amplifier with a noise figure of 5 dB and a PIN 
photodiode, which has an active area of 1 cm² and 0.6 A/W responsivity.
Though it is usual to have optical concentrators or optical lenses used to enhance opti-
cal power received by a conventional LiFi receiver, an optical amplifier has been added 
here only to permit sensitivity analysis by simulation and analysis of high-range opera -
tion. Similar optical wireless works based on simulations have employed the EDFA 
pre-amplifiers in front of the photodiode to enhance the performance of receivers in 
turbulence and scintillation, also shown by Dawuti et al. [ 27]. The idealized gain mod -
elled as an optical amplifier is a gain mechanism that is used to amplify the sensitivity of 
the receiver. In real-world VLC receivers, the front end is made up of a PIN photodiode 
and a transimpedance amplifier (TIA). During hardware prototyping, a complete analog 
receiver chain will be described.
To ensure the simulation environment achieves the maximum received optical power 
in taking long-range indoor links, the choice of a 1 cm 2 photodiode is simply made to 
ensure the highest received optical power. Though the large area photodiodes generally 
have lower bandwidth than smaller devices because of increased junction capacitance, 
recent designs of VLC receivers have shown that large area photodiodes with band -
widths extending to 500–800  MHz can be realized through optimized device designs. 
The future hardware development will use correctly bandwidth-optimized PDs in order 
to meet hospital-grade Gbps.
The optical amplifier includes a polarization filter to reduce gain variations caused 
by polarization while simultaneously stopping external light from harming system 
Page 8 of 21
Sharma et al. Discover Computing           (2026) 29:30 
performance. An OFDM-QAM demodulator with zero-forcing equalization enables data 
recovery. The channel estimation technique used in this study is zero-forcing (ZF) equal-
ization because of its low complexity and appropriateness for real-time medical com -
munication. For increased robustness under various indoor optical conditions, future 
work will expand the analysis to include MMSE and pilot-aided estimation schemes. The 
selection of the PIN photodiode is based on its capability to maintain low noise levels. 
The downlink LiFi channel is the research theme of the present paper. Futuristic work 
will involve an uplink solution, which will probably be built on eye-safe infrared trans -
mission, power levels, interference handling, and medical quality safety standards. This 
design ensures stable reception under EMI, ambient light variation, and patient move -
ment—conditions that typically degrade LiFi performance in hospitals.

sections.title: 3 Mathematical modelling and comprehensive analysis
sections.text:
In this section, the theory behind the mathematical framework of the evaluation of the 
proposed LiFi system will be presented, making sure that all the design decisions made 
are quantitatively supported and can be applied to realistic conditions in the hospital 
context. The models deal with the BER, SNR, optical power, and channel characteristics 
so that the evaluation can be reproducible and clinically meaningful.

sections.title: 4 Results and discussion
sections.text:
In this section, the simulation results are discussed to show that the proposed system 
using 4QAM-OFDM LiFi can perform better by providing improved BER, spectral effi -
ciency, EMI immunity, and biological safety as compared to the current systems avail -
able in hospitals. Every finding is referred to its upgrade or downgrade effect on the 
dependability and safety of the hospital network.

sections.title: 4.1 OFDM and quadrature modulator (QM) spectral analysis
sections.text:
The spectral evaluation of both OFDM and QM signals in Fig.  2 shows their potential 
use in hospital-based LiFi systems. These findings affirm that the recommended system 
has a stable power spectral density of 1024 subcarriers, which would provide a consis -
tent high-speed data transfer with no interference to the medical devices.
Page 12 of 21
Sharma et al. Discover Computing           (2026) 29:30 
The spectrum analysis of OFDM and QM signals proves that high-speed LiFi works 
well for hospital settings by managing interference and optimizing efficiency in the spec-
trum. The OFDM spectrum covers the 1 GHz bandwidth from 0 to 1 GHz and provides a 
stable power spectral density distribution for its 1024 subcarriers. The use of maximum 
power output (20–30 dBm) supports up to 1 Gbps data rates, which fulfil the needs of a 
real-time medical imaging patient monitoring application.
The QM signal measures 1 GHz at its centre and extends power gradually across fre -
quencies greater than 4 GHz. The designed structure maintains phase integrity with less 
than 0.5° phase error to reduce inter-symbol interference (ISI) in hospital environments 
with multipath reflections. The QM spectrum maintains compatibility for optical con -
version, which enables smooth implementation with LiFi-based illumination systems to 
offer efficient RF-based telemetry replacement.
The distinct separation between OFDM and QM spectra ensures zero overlap with fre-
quency bands used by sensitive hospital equipment, strengthening EMI immunity. The 
implementation of OFDM-QM architecture based on LiFi technology within hospital 
communication networks provides strong EMI protection that maintains data protec -
tion, together with fast delivery speed and healthcare safety requirements. The proposed 
OFDM-QM LiFi design offers effective high-speed data transmission without interfer -
ence, so it represents a suitable choice for future wireless medical network development.

sections.title: 4.2 Quadrature modulator and demodulator output analysis
sections.text:
The spectrum analysis results for the quadrature modulator and demodulator shown in 
Fig. 3 prove that LiFi signals can be successfully transmitted and recovered inside hos -
pital settings. The frequency domain analysis of the quadrature modulator (QM) output 
(left panel) confirms successful modulation of the 4QAM signal onto a 1  GHz carrier 
frequency.
Fig. 2 Spectrum of OFDM and QM obtained from MATLAB simulation
 
Page 13 of 21
Sharma et al. Discover Computing           (2026) 29:30 
A strong single peak appears at 1 GHz within the spectrum, which signifies effective 
baseband information conversion. The modulation procedure generates the communi -
cation signal for optical conversion, which operates within LiFi-based transmission net -
works by minimizing disturbances during transmission. The right panel output of the 
quadrature demodulator recovers the signal at baseband frequency (0  Hz), therefore 
maintaining both original spectral composition and equal power distribution. Signal 
demodulation occurs without significant distortion because the power levels stay consis-
tent across the bandwidth of the spectrum. The LiFi transmission stability and interfer -
ence-free nature can be supported by an absence of noticeable spectral leakage together 
with preserved original signal structure, which enables its suitability as a high-speed and 
EMI-resilient communication method in hospital settings.
The results show that quadrature amplitude modulation and demodulation work effi -
ciently to maintain signal integrity by minimizing phase distortion, enabling high data 
accuracy needed for medical imaging. This ensures accurate, lossless transfer of MRI 
scans, CT images, and other diagnostic datasets without risk of corruption.

sections.title: 4.3 LED and LOS optical spectrum analysis
sections.text:
The operational functionality of the LiFi transmitter LED and receiver LOS system with 
amplification in hospital settings can be verified through optical spectrum analysis. The 
LED generates power at 500  nm wavelength, which produces green light in the range 
between − 5 dBm to 30 dBm, as shown in Fig.  4. A flat spectrum across 489–503  nm 
indicates stable optical output. The LED noise floor reaches the approximate value of 
−100 dBm, allowing low interference with sensitive medical equipment, thus maintain -
ing EMI safety in hospital environments.
The output spectrum of the LOS LiFi system output spectrum with an optical amplifier 
(bottom panel) achieves successful signal reception over longer distances, as is shown in 
Fig. 4. The received optical power spans vary from − 20 dBm to 10 dBm, whereas using 
a + 20 dB gain of the optical amplifier allows handling the path loss resulting from patient 
movement and medical equipment interference. The LOS output spectrum presents a 
slightly expanded signal spectrum covering the 494 to 503 nm range that improves sig -
nal stability without compromising compatibility with medical-grade optical receivers. 
The low noise floor of −50 dBm demonstrates excellent resistance to background light 
Fig. 3 Quadrature modulator/demodulator output
 
Page 14 of 21
Sharma et al. Discover Computing           (2026) 29:30 
interference, thus making it appropriate for ICU and hospital corridor environments 
with their need for highly reliable LiFi communication.

Simulation parameters of the proposed LiFi system
